modules.title: AI in our cyber work: colleague showcase
modules.why: Generic courses cannot establish actual bank adoption.
modules.agenda: Three worked cases and cross-domain discussion; distinguish production, restricted pilots and horizon ideas.
modules.evidence: Explain one own-domain and one adjacent-domain case, limits and changed human work.
modules.prerequisites: Verified case owners, sanitised evidence and approved status labels.

modules.title: Approved platform, architecture and safe use
modules.why: Teach the actual model, agent, connector, permission and data boundaries.
modules.agenda: Architecture walkthrough, data classification choices, permissions and a stop/escalation demonstration.
modules.evidence: Trace a request across model, tools and data; choose safe inputs and identify the accountable owner.
modules.prerequisites: Approved architecture and data/access guidance; simulation if learner access is unavailable.

modules.title: AI limitations, bank attack examples and knowledge check
modules.why: Use bank examples for current limitations, spoofing and AI-enabled attacks.
modules.agenda: Use sanitised or clearly labelled illustrative bank attack cases (N5.4), recognise AI-enabled intrusion, examine planted false outputs and practise independent identity verification. Deepfakes are a brief impersonation example within social engineering. Finish with a knowledge check and feedback.
modules.evidence: Recognise unsupported output and suspicious content, explain uncertainty, identify the bank attack scenario and choose independent trusted-channel verification or escalation.
modules.prerequisites: Current sanitised cases, answer key and support route.

modules.title: Overview of AI security risks
modules.owner: Cyber awareness lead + AI security architect
modules.why: Give every cyber employee a coherent risk map before specialist depth. Keep this separate from N5.4 bank attack examples and N4 employee responsible-use rules.
modules.agenda: Explain six risk families: instruction manipulation, disclosure, unsafe output handling, excessive permissions/actions, compromised components/sources, and service disruption/resource consumption. Use a short scenario for each, connect it to a precaution or escalation, and check recognition. Use current OWASP LLM and agentic guidance as trainer references; no framework-ID memorisation or exploitation lab.
modules.evidence: Learner categorises short scenarios, explains the consequence and selects the appropriate precaution/escalation. Pilot and assess the module against N5.8 before awarding coverage credit.
modules.prerequisites: Trainer-reviewed OWASP risk map, answer key, approved escalation route and accessible examples.

modules.title: Responsible AI-assisted work case
modules.why: A generic app project is insufficient evidence of bank work.
modules.agenda: 30m task/model/context setup; 60m supported task with reset and verification; 30m review and handover.
modules.evidence: Produce a sourced work result, correct a planted error, manage session context and retain responsibility.
modules.prerequisites: Approved tool or realistic simulator, safe task data, answer criteria.

modules.title: Supervise, intervene and recover

modules.evidence: Correctly delegate, monitor, intervene, recover and record the human decision.
modules.prerequisites: Seeded failure traces, validated recovery path, scoped permissions.
